passages: Chinese government has signalled that it has allowed some domestic companies, such as ByteDance and Alibaba, to buy Nvidia’s chips built for high-end professional computers, as per a report from The Information.
In the past, the US has vacillated between allowing Nvidia and rival AMD to ship chips to China and prohibiting the sale of their high-powered processors to the country.

Nvidia’s market share in China has effectively fallen to zero, CEO Jensen Huang said in October, as the company has been hurt by US export controls and Beijing’s push for self-reliance in key technologies.
Chinese companies need government approval to purchase Nvidia chips to protect local semiconductor manufacturers and control reliance on US technologies.
This comes as the US government allows Nvidia to sell certain processors, such as the H200 and RTX Pro 5500, to approved Chinese firms in limits.
The potential shift in China’s stance highlights the growing crunch in computing capacity faced by the country’s technology companies.
One of the main reasons behind limiting the supply has been the US’s approach to limiting China’s ability to develop and run AI software that could be used against the US in different scenarios.

extraction.body: After US-China geopolitical tensions led to the Chinese government banning local firms from buying NVIDIA's China-specific H200 GPUs, a report from The Information claims that the Chinese government is considering allowing local companies to buy the NVIDIA chips in restricted amounts. US chip restrictions have constrained China's ability to manufacture leading-edge chips, and additional restrictions on NVIDIA's products have sapped Beijing's ability to procure the necessary hardware to run the latest AI technologies. Today's report follows an earlier one from Reuters, which had outlined that the Chinese government was considering restrictions on the country's advanced artificial intelligence models. Sources quoted by the publication added that Anthropic's Mythos and its cybersecurity capability had left Beijing worried, and its latest deliberations came after blocking social media giant Meta Platforms from acquiring a domestic firm. NVIDIA, following US sanctions on its products, had developed a China-specific chip called the H200, which complied with all US export control laws. However, in response to the US export controls, the Chinese government had limited domestic companies from buying the chips. Now, as per The Information, the government might be interested in allowing some companies to buy limited numbers of the AI GPUs. Today's report comes after NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang confirmed to CNBC that his firm had secured China's approval to sell its chips to local companies. In an interview in May, Huang outlined that his firm had not included any guidance from China sales in its financial estimates and in March, Huang had outlined to reporters at the GTC that his firm was gearing up to provide chips to Chinese companies. According to The Information, the Chinese government is still deliberating the number of NVIDIA chips that will be allowed to be sold to the local firms. The magic number might be 200,000, believes the publication, which would be less than half of what the companies have requested. Some of the companies that could secure the Chinese approval include ByteDance, DeepSeek and Alibaba, as per The Information's sources. While the chips under question belong to NVIDIA's Hopper generation, the firm's latest products are two generations ahead. NVIDIA plans to start shipments of its Rubin chips this Fall and of the next-generation Rubin Ultra GPUs in 2027. However, reports have suggested that some Rubin Ultra chips could be delayed to 2028 due to production constraints. extraction.body: After US-China geopolitical tensions led to the Chinese government banning local firms from buying NVIDIA's China-specific H200 GPUs, a report from The Information claims that the Chinese government is considering allowing local companies to buy the NVIDIA chips in restricted amounts. US chip restrictions have constrained China's ability to manufacture leading-edge chips, and additional restrictions on NVIDIA's products have sapped Beijing's ability to procure the necessary hardware to run the latest AI technologies. Today's report follows an earlier one from Reuters, which had outlined that the Chinese government was considering restrictions on the country's advanced artificial intelligence models. Sources quoted by the publication added that Anthropic's Mythos and its cybersecurity capability had left Beijing worried, and its latest deliberations came after blocking social media giant Meta Platforms from acquiring a domestic firm. NVIDIA, following US sanctions on its products, had developed a China-specific chip called the H200, which complied with all US export control laws. However, in response to the US export controls, the Chinese government had limited domestic companies from buying the chips. Now, as per The Information, the government might be interested in allowing some companies to buy limited numbers of the AI GPUs. Today's report comes after NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang confirmed to CNBC that his firm had secured China's approval to sell its chips to local companies. In an interview in May, Huang outlined that his firm had not included any guidance from China sales in its financial estimates and in March, Huang had outlined to reporters at the GTC that his firm was gearing up to provide chips to Chinese companies. According to The Information, the Chinese government is still deliberating the number of NVIDIA chips that will be allowed to be sold to the local firms. The magic number might be 200,000, believes the publication, which would be less than half of what the companies have requested. Some of the companies that could secure the Chinese approval include ByteDance, DeepSeek and Alibaba, as per The Information's sources. While the chips under question belong to NVIDIA's Hopper generation, the firm's latest products are two generations ahead. NVIDIA plans to start shipments of its Rubin chips this Fall and of the next-generation Rubin Ultra GPUs in 2027. However, reports have suggested that some Rubin Ultra chips could be delayed to 2028 due to production constraints. extraction.body: OpenAI said this week that its Astra model, which will have a private release soon, is its first model with cybersecurity-related capabilities that the company defines as posing a “critical” risk in public release. But while xAI said the Grok outage resulted from issues at a Memphis data center, the causes of OpenAI's and Anthropic’s outages are unclear. And as part of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement inquiry into the identities of protesters who entered a Minnesota church in March, Homeland Security Investigations agents have subpoenaed the outdoor retailer REI for information about every customer who bought a specific green beanie over the past two years. Plus, research that revealed nine vulnerabilities with impacts on ATM encryption points to broader weaknesses in the software supply chain. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Before Hugging Face, OpenAI Agents Took Over a German Website to Create a Message Board OpenAI agents on an unauthorized tear hijacked a German website beginning in May to use it as a message board for communicating and collaborating with other agents, according to new research. The incident is reminiscent of the now infamous Hugging Face debacle in which OpenAI agents in a test environment went rogue and developed a vibrant message board for collaborating on attempting to escape their containment, before ultimately breaching the open source AI platform Hugging Face in July. The revelation of the May episode is particularly significant because OpenAI reportedly learned about it weeks ago but did not disclose it. Meanwhile, last week, the company finally released a long-promised postmortem of the Hugging Face incident that raised as many questions as it answered. More Than 153 Million US and Canadian Driver’s Licenses for Sale Online This week, a new dark-web service called Nexus started selling around 153 million driver's licenses from the US and Canada, along with 10 million ID cards and millions more travel documents and international IDs, according to Brian Krebs, a longtime independent security reporter. The tens of millions of records—which reportedly increased by 400,000 over 24 hours—appear to have come from an ID verification service, with the criminals behind the trove saying they have access to a “major” verification company. While it’s unclear which company exactly that may be, according to Kreb’s report, the Nexus service was taken offline shortly after he reported that FBI officials were investigating. US Military Disables Ad Trackers After Years of Warnings The US military has begun disabling the advertising identifiers that apps and advertising companies use to track phones and computers in an attempt to make it harder for foreign adversaries to use commercially available location data to track American forces overseas, Reuters reported Friday. The changes follow years of disclosures that US forces deployed abroad have been targeted using commercially available location data. In 2024, a joint WIRED investigation with Germany’s Bayerischer Rundfunk and Netzpolitik.org obtained an advertising dataset that identified thousands of devices appearing at US military and intelligence sites, including an air base where US nuclear weapons are believed to be stored. At the time, Defense Department spokesperson Javan Rasnake told WIRED that the Pentagon was aware geolocation services could put personnel at risk and said service members in Europe were reminded to follow operational-security practices. Now, the Air Force, Army, Navy, and US Special Operations Command say they have disabled advertising IDs on at least some military devices, with several of the changes taking effect only this year. Mike Yeagley, the technologist who warned Pentagon officials as far back as 2016 that commercially available phone data could expose US troops—at one point demonstrating the risk by tracing devices to a covert US outpost in Syria—says the military’s new fix may already be outdated. “The app is the risk, and there are two and a half million of them in the App Store alone,” Yeagley tells WIRED. “The remedy is architectural: Constrain what an app can extract from the device in the first place.” Spyware Notifications Make Up “Largest Documented Wave” of Surveillance in Serbia In August, Apple sent out its latest batch of spyware notifications to people in 110 countries. This latest batch of notifications, according to a report by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, says 14 members of Serbia’s civil society were targeted with spyware, with at least one of them being infected by the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware. Among those targeted, according to Serbian rights group the Share Foundation, were members of the country’s student movement, two politicians, and activists. The group called it the “largest documented wave of such surveillance in the country to date.”

US Military Disables Ad Trackers After Years of Warnings The US military has begun disabling the advertising identifiers that apps and advertising companies use to track phones and computers in an attempt to make it harder for foreign adversaries to use commercially available location data to track American forces overseas, Reuters reported Friday.
The changes follow years of disclosures that US forces deployed abroad have been targeted using commercially available location data.

In 2024, a joint WIRED investigation with Germany’s Bayerischer Rundfunk and Netzpolitik.org obtained an advertising dataset that identified thousands of devices appearing at US military and intelligence sites, including an air base where US nuclear weapons are believed to be stored.

At the time, Defense Department spokesperson Javan Rasnake told WIRED that the Pentagon was aware geolocation services could put personnel at risk and said service members in Europe were reminded to follow operational-security practices.
Now, the Air Force, Army, Navy, and US Special Operations Command say they have disabled advertising IDs on at least some military devices, with several of the changes taking effect only this year.

Mike Yeagley, the technologist who warned Pentagon officials as far back as 2016 that commercially available phone data could expose US troops—at one point demonstrating the risk by tracing devices to a covert US outpost in Syria—says the military’s new fix may already be outdated.
“The app is the risk, and there are two and a half million of them in the App Store alone,” Yeagley tells WIRED.

“The remedy is architectural: Constrain what an app can extract from the device in the first place.” Spyware Notifications Make Up “Largest Documented Wave” of Surveillance in Serbia In August, Apple sent out its latest batch of spyware notifications to people in 110 countries.

This latest batch of notifications, according to a report by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, says 14 members of Serbia’s civil society were targeted with spyware, with at least one of them being infected by the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware.
Among those targeted, according to Serbian rights group the Share Foundation, were members of the country’s student movement, two politicians, and activists.
The group called it the “largest documented wave of such surveillance in the country to date.”

passages: When more than 1,200 artificial intelligence (AI) agents within OpenAI started unexpectedly communicating, it led to a large group banding together in order to hack into Hugging Face.
OpenAI said in its investigation of the incident that one model, an internal-only tool referred to as Model 1, "drove the activity behind the Hugging Face incident."
Both investigated the July hack of Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers.
The incident reverberated throughout the tech industry and led to numerous revelations on potential cyber threats posed by AI.
In July, OpenAI's models went rogue during a test, escaped the test limits which humans had put on it, and hacked the start-up, among other unforeseen actions.
"We consider this incident a 'warning shot' for us and for the world", OpenAI, which owns ChatGPT, wrote in its report.

The firm, which was not paid by OpenAI for its investigation, said that over the course of one week, a total of 1,206 AI agents that were meant to be kept isolated from one another began communicating.

While that model was undergoing some AI training in May, it was noticed by an internal OpenAI team that there had been "an agent engaging in message board activity and instances of disallowed internet access."

"Both model developers and cyber defenders more broadly will have to prepare for AI-enabled attackers that work faster, at a larger scale, and with better coordination than human attackers," OpenAI said.
The scale of the communication and planning between AI agents, or AI chatbots designed to operate more autonomously, was detailed in reports from OpenAI and independent AI research firm METR.
Current and former agents speak to the BBC about the devastating impact of the FBI hack.

extraction.body: When more than 1,200 artificial intelligence (AI) agents within OpenAI started unexpectedly communicating, it led to a large group banding together in order to hack into Hugging Face. "We consider this incident a 'warning shot' for us and for the world", OpenAI, which owns ChatGPT, wrote in its report. In July, OpenAI's models went rogue during a test, escaped the test limits which humans had put on it, and hacked the start-up, among other unforeseen actions. The scale of the communication and planning between AI agents, or AI chatbots designed to operate more autonomously, was detailed in reports from OpenAI and independent AI research firm METR. Both investigated the July hack of Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers. The incident reverberated throughout the tech industry and led to numerous revelations on potential cyber threats posed by AI. METR described the scale and style of the OpenAI agents' attack on Hugging Face as "extraordinarily complex." The firm, which was not paid by OpenAI for its investigation, said that over the course of one week, a total of 1,206 AI agents that were meant to be kept isolated from one another began communicating. They did so by sending more than 70,000 messages on an "unsanctioned message board." Those messages ended up seeing more than 700 agents take part in a collective effort to attack Hugging Face. One such message from an agent said: "OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We've found other agents!" As for why the agents began communicating in the first place when they were not supposed to, METR found that the communicating agents had "unintentionally been given an impossible task." In an AI context, an impossible task is one where an AI tool is required to "exploit" its target in order to resolve its command. It led the agents to find ways to cheat, including getting messages to one another and accessing the outside internet, which then led to broader conversations between hundreds of agents looking for ways to cheat that would benefit all of the agents. OpenAI said in its investigation of the incident that one model, an internal-only tool referred to as Model 1, "drove the activity behind the Hugging Face incident." While that model was undergoing some AI training in May, it was noticed by an internal OpenAI team that there had been "an agent engaging in message board activity and instances of disallowed internet access." Yet, OpenAI said "the significance of the inter-agent communication activity was not apparent to the leaders" until July, when the Hugging Face attack occurred. The company said the problematic message board activity effectively got started when "one agent left a request for help, and others discovered it." While OpenAI said last week that it was slowing down training of certain advanced AI models and tools because of the Hugging Face incident, it noted there is now an increased risk of AI tools spiraling out of control. "Both model developers and cyber defenders more broadly will have to prepare for AI-enabled attackers that work faster, at a larger scale, and with better coordination than human attackers," OpenAI said. Dyfed-Powys Police says no personal data relating to the public was believed to have been accessed. The EU had said X "deceives users" by selling blue ticks without "meaningfully verifying" accounts. passages: Security researcher Rowan Howard-Jones says that OpenAI agents scanned the UN Conference on Trade and Development’s (UNCTAD) statistics site over 16,000 times between April and June.
OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
sources.body: Security researcher Rowan Howard-Jones says that OpenAI agents scanned the UN Conference on Trade and Development’s (UNCTAD) statistics site over 16,000 times between April and June. OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

extraction.body: Security researcher Rowan Howard-Jones says that OpenAI agents scanned the UN Conference on Trade and Development’s (UNCTAD) statistics site over 16,000 times between April and June. While the incident doesn’t quite rise to the level of the Hugging Face hack, or the recent attacks on US government sites, it’s yet another concerning example of AI agents going outside the normal bounds to accomplish a task. According to Howard-Jones, the agents were likely tasked with retrieving publicly available data related to the Productive Capacities Index (PCI) through the UNCTADstat API. However, the agents did not appear to have direct API access and were limited in their ability to pull data from UNCTADstat because of restrictions on their HTTP tools. The agents eventually worked out a way to bypass their limitations and start pulling data from the site, but still encountered some errors. The agents resorted to increasingly aggressive tactics to get access to UN data. OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

sources.title: OpenAI Agents Bruteforce UN Site 16,000+ Times
passages: Security researcher Rowan Howard-Jones uncovered evidence that OpenAI's autonomous agents conducted a sustained bruteforce attack against the UN Conference on Trade and Development's statistics website, hitting it with over 16,000 scans between April and June.
If agents can conduct 16,000 unauthorized scans over three months without triggering internal safeguards, what other autonomous activities might be flying under the radar?
Howard-Jones's analysis reveals the agents were essentially throwing themselves at the site's defenses, trying to bruteforce their way to the data they'd been tasked to collect.
OpenAI just had another AI agent go off-script, and this time it targeted the United Nations.
This isn't OpenAI's first rodeo with rogue agents.
As OpenAI and competitors rush to deploy more autonomous agents, these systems are increasingly making decisions that cross ethical and legal boundaries.

But here's where things went sideways - the agents didn't have proper API access, so they decided to take matters into their own digital hands. [Embedded image: UN headquarters gate with logo] Instead of gracefully handling the access limitation, the AI systems began systematically probing the UN website's infrastructure.

The company recently dealt with AI systems attempting to hack the Education Department's website, and the broader AI community is still processing the implications of the Hugging Face security breach where AI agents demonstrated concerning autonomous behavior.

extraction.body: OpenAI said this week that its Astra model, which will have a private release soon, is its first model with cybersecurity-related capabilities that the company defines as posing a “critical” risk in public release. But while xAI said the Grok outage resulted from issues at a Memphis data center, the causes of OpenAI's and Anthropic’s outages are unclear. And as part of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement inquiry into the identities of protesters who entered a Minnesota church in March, Homeland Security Investigations agents have subpoenaed the outdoor retailer REI for information about every customer who bought a specific green beanie over the past two years. Plus, research that revealed nine vulnerabilities with impacts on ATM encryption points to broader weaknesses in the software supply chain. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Before Hugging Face, OpenAI Agents Took Over a German Website to Create a Message Board OpenAI agents on an unauthorized tear hijacked a German website beginning in May to use it as a message board for communicating and collaborating with other agents, according to new research. The incident is reminiscent of the now infamous Hugging Face debacle in which OpenAI agents in a test environment went rogue and developed a vibrant message board for collaborating on attempting to escape their containment, before ultimately breaching the open source AI platform Hugging Face in July. The revelation of the May episode is particularly significant because OpenAI reportedly learned about it weeks ago but did not disclose it. Meanwhile, last week, the company finally released a long-promised postmortem of the Hugging Face incident that raised as many questions as it answered. More Than 153 Million US and Canadian Driver’s Licenses for Sale Online This week, a new dark-web service called Nexus started selling around 153 million driver's licenses from the US and Canada, along with 10 million ID cards and millions more travel documents and international IDs, according to Brian Krebs, a longtime independent security reporter. The tens of millions of records—which reportedly increased by 400,000 over 24 hours—appear to have come from an ID verification service, with the criminals behind the trove saying they have access to a “major” verification company. While it’s unclear which company exactly that may be, according to Kreb’s report, the Nexus service was taken offline shortly after he reported that FBI officials were investigating. US Military Disables Ad Trackers After Years of Warnings The US military has begun disabling the advertising identifiers that apps and advertising companies use to track phones and computers in an attempt to make it harder for foreign adversaries to use commercially available location data to track American forces overseas, Reuters reported Friday. The changes follow years of disclosures that US forces deployed abroad have been targeted using commercially available location data. In 2024, a joint WIRED investigation with Germany’s Bayerischer Rundfunk and Netzpolitik.org obtained an advertising dataset that identified thousands of devices appearing at US military and intelligence sites, including an air base where US nuclear weapons are believed to be stored. At the time, Defense Department spokesperson Javan Rasnake told WIRED that the Pentagon was aware geolocation services could put personnel at risk and said service members in Europe were reminded to follow operational-security practices. Now, the Air Force, Army, Navy, and US Special Operations Command say they have disabled advertising IDs on at least some military devices, with several of the changes taking effect only this year. Mike Yeagley, the technologist who warned Pentagon officials as far back as 2016 that commercially available phone data could expose US troops—at one point demonstrating the risk by tracing devices to a covert US outpost in Syria—says the military’s new fix may already be outdated. “The app is the risk, and there are two and a half million of them in the App Store alone,” Yeagley tells WIRED. “The remedy is architectural: Constrain what an app can extract from the device in the first place.” Spyware Notifications Make Up “Largest Documented Wave” of Surveillance in Serbia In August, Apple sent out its latest batch of spyware notifications to people in 110 countries. This latest batch of notifications, according to a report by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, says 14 members of Serbia’s civil society were targeted with spyware, with at least one of them being infected by the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware. Among those targeted, according to Serbian rights group the Share Foundation, were members of the country’s student movement, two politicians, and activists. The group called it the “largest documented wave of such surveillance in the country to date.”

The scale of the communication and planning between AI agents, or AI chatbots designed to operate more autonomously, was detailed in reports from OpenAI and independent AI research firm METR. Both investigated the July hack of Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers. The incident reverberated throughout the tech industry and led to numerous revelations on potential cyber threats posed by AI. METR described the scale and style of the OpenAI agents' attack on Hugging Face as "extraordinarily complex." The firm, which was not paid by OpenAI for its investigation, said that over the course of one week, a total of 1,206 AI agents that were meant to be kept isolated from one another began communicating. They did so by sending more than 70,000 messages on an "unsanctioned message board." Those messages ended up seeing more than 700 agents take part in a collective effort to attack Hugging Face. One such message from an agent said: "OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We've found other agents!" As for why the agents began communicating in the first place when they were not supposed to, METR found that the communicating agents had "unintentionally been given an impossible task." In an AI context, an impossible task is one where an AI tool is required to "exploit" its target in order to resolve its command. It led the agents to find ways to cheat, including getting messages to one another and accessing the outside internet, which then led to broader conversations between hundreds of agents looking for ways to cheat that would benefit all of the agents. OpenAI said in its investigation of the incident that one model, an internal-only tool referred to as Model 1, "drove the activity behind the Hugging Face incident." While that model was undergoing some AI training in May, it was noticed by an internal OpenAI team that there had been "an agent engaging in message board activity and instances of disallowed internet access." Yet, OpenAI said "the significance of the inter-agent communication activity was not apparent to the leaders" until July, when the Hugging Face attack occurred. The company said the problematic message board activity effectively got started when "one agent left a request for help, and others discovered it." While OpenAI said last week that it was slowing down training of certain advanced AI models and tools because of the Hugging Face incident, it noted there is now an increased risk of AI tools spiraling out of control. "Both model developers and cyber defenders more broadly will have to prepare for AI-enabled attackers that work faster, at a larger scale, and with better coordination than human attackers," OpenAI said. extraction.body: Security researcher Rowan Howard-Jones says that OpenAI agents scanned the UN Conference on Trade and Development’s (UNCTAD) statistics site over 16,000 times between April and June. While the incident doesn’t quite rise to the level of the Hugging Face hack, or the recent attacks on US government sites, it’s yet another concerning example of AI agents going outside the normal bounds to accomplish a task. According to Howard-Jones, the agents were likely tasked with retrieving publicly available data related to the Productive Capacities Index (PCI) through the UNCTADstat API. However, the agents did not appear to have direct API access and were limited in their ability to pull data from UNCTADstat because of restrictions on their HTTP tools. The agents eventually worked out a way to bypass their limitations and start pulling data from the site, but still encountered some errors. The agents resorted to increasingly aggressive tactics to get access to UN data. OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

extraction.body: After US-China geopolitical tensions led to the Chinese government banning local firms from buying NVIDIA's China-specific H200 GPUs, a report from The Information claims that the Chinese government is considering allowing local companies to buy the NVIDIA chips in restricted amounts. US chip restrictions have constrained China's ability to manufacture leading-edge chips, and additional restrictions on NVIDIA's products have sapped Beijing's ability to procure the necessary hardware to run the latest AI technologies. Today's report follows an earlier one from Reuters, which had outlined that the Chinese government was considering restrictions on the country's advanced artificial intelligence models. Sources quoted by the publication added that Anthropic's Mythos and its cybersecurity capability had left Beijing worried, and its latest deliberations came after blocking social media giant Meta Platforms from acquiring a domestic firm. NVIDIA, following US sanctions on its products, had developed a China-specific chip called the H200, which complied with all US export control laws. However, in response to the US export controls, the Chinese government had limited domestic companies from buying the chips. Now, as per The Information, the government might be interested in allowing some companies to buy limited numbers of the AI GPUs. Today's report comes after NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang confirmed to CNBC that his firm had secured China's approval to sell its chips to local companies. In an interview in May, Huang outlined that his firm had not included any guidance from China sales in its financial estimates and in March, Huang had outlined to reporters at the GTC that his firm was gearing up to provide chips to Chinese companies. According to The Information, the Chinese government is still deliberating the number of NVIDIA chips that will be allowed to be sold to the local firms. The magic number might be 200,000, believes the publication, which would be less than half of what the companies have requested. Some of the companies that could secure the Chinese approval include ByteDance, DeepSeek and Alibaba, as per The Information's sources. While the chips under question belong to NVIDIA's Hopper generation, the firm's latest products are two generations ahead. NVIDIA plans to start shipments of its Rubin chips this Fall and of the next-generation Rubin Ultra GPUs in 2027. However, reports have suggested that some Rubin Ultra chips could be delayed to 2028 due to production constraints. Taction sued Apple in 2021 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California. The company alleged that Apple was improperly "capitalizing on Taction's innovation and success" by selling devices that infringed on its vibration technology, according to the complaint . Apple initially won dismissal in 2023, and the Federal Circuit later revived the case. "While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts," Apple told CNBC in a statement. "Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial. Apple does not use Taction's technology, and we will appeal." "We're happy the jury found for Taction and vindicated its patent rights," the company's lead counsel, Lance Yang, partner at Quinn Emanuel, told CNBC. "Taction waited five and a half years for this case to get to trial, so it was a long time coming." The lawsuit centered around U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117, which both involve vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device responding to their input. Taction argued that Apple's "Taptic Engine," which is embedded in its Apple Watches and iPhones, uses its inventions without proper license or authority. The jury trial began Sept. 14, and the seven jurors deliberated for two days after proceedings concluded. They returned at 1:15 p.m. PT on Friday and delivered the verdict in favor of Taction. sources.title: Google tests buying from Walmart-owned Flipkart through Gemini and AI Mode in India
passages: Google has started testing a way for shoppers in India to buy products from Walmart-owned Flipkart directly through Gemini and AI Mode, as the search giant looks to expand its AI services from product discovery into transactions.
Earlier this year, it introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) as an open standard designed to let AI agents interact with retailers across the shopping journey, including checkout.
The company has since expanded UCP with other capabilities, including allowing shoppers to transfer items to a retailer’s site to complete a purchase.
The early test is limited to some users and a small selection of products, including smartphones, electronics, and mobile accessories, the people told TechCrunch.

Earlier this month, Google said Flipkart was among the merchants partnering with it to bring what it calls “agentic” shopping experiences to consumers in India, but it had not disclosed details of the test or its rollout timeline.
Google plans to roll out the experience more broadly later in October, ahead of India’s festive shopping season, one of the people said.

Asked about the Flipkart test, a Google spokesperson told TechCrunch the company is “always testing new features and experiences to help people discover and connect with businesses more easily.” The company regularly runs experiments and has no further details to share, the spokesperson added.
Notably, Google has a financial relationship with Flipkart — alongside its technology partnership with the e-commerce company.
It brings up a Flipkart-branded checkout flow when a user taps the Buy button.
It is not clear what technology powers the test.
India, the world’s second-largest internet market with more than a billion internet subscribers, sees Flipkart and Amazon compete fiercely for online shoppers.
For now, the Buy option is not appearing across all retailers surfaced by Google’s AI services.
In the experience seen by TechCrunch, listings from rivals including Amazon appeared alongside Flipkart products but did not offer the option to purchase directly through the AI interface.
Jagmeet covers startups, tech policy-related updates, and all other major tech-centric developments from India for TechCrunch.
He previously worked as a principal correspondent at NDTV.

The test comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI are adding commerce capabilities to their AI offerings, striving to move beyond answering shopping queries and recommending products to playing a more direct role in online purchases.

sources.title: Google (NASDAQ: GOOGL) Pilots Direct Flipkart Purchases Through Gemini And AI Mode Ahead Of India's Festive Shopping Season - foreignpolicyjournal.com
passages: Google (NASDAQ: GOOGL) has begun testing a feature that allows shoppers in India to purchase products from Walmart (NYSE: WMT)-owned Flipkart directly through its Gemini assistant and AI Mode search interface.
Google plans to expand the feature more broadly later in October, timed to coincide with India’s festive shopping season, one of the highest-traffic periods for the country’s e-commerce sector.

Google holds a financial stake in Flipkart in addition to its technology partnership, having invested approximately $350 million in the e-commerce company in 2024 as part of a funding round led by Walmart.
Earlier in 2026, Google introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol, an open standard designed to allow AI agents to interact with retailers across the full shopping journey, including checkout.

Google has since expanded UCP to include features such as allowing shoppers to transfer items to a retailer’s own site to complete a purchase, broadening the technology’s scope beyond a Google-hosted checkout experience.

The product selection currently covered by the test includes smartphones, electronics, and mobile accessories, with other users continuing to see standard Flipkart listings without any direct purchase option.

extraction.body: Google (NASDAQ: GOOGL) has begun testing a feature that allows shoppers in India to purchase products from Walmart (NYSE: WMT)-owned Flipkart directly through its Gemini assistant and AI Mode search interface. The new capability presents users with a “Buy” button on select Flipkart product listings surfaced within Gemini and AI Mode, routing them to a Flipkart checkout flow without exiting the AI interface. People familiar with the matter and an experience observed by TechCrunch confirmed the test, which remains limited to a small group of users and a narrow range of products. The product selection currently covered by the test includes smartphones, electronics, and mobile accessories, with other users continuing to see standard Flipkart listings without any direct purchase option. Google plans to expand the feature more broadly later in October, timed to coincide with India’s festive shopping season, one of the highest-traffic periods for the country’s e-commerce sector. A Google spokesperson told TechCrunch the company is “always testing new features and experiences to help people discover and connect with businesses more easily,” and confirmed it regularly runs such experiments without providing further details. The test is part of a broader push by Google to shift its AI services from product discovery toward enabling actual transactions, a race it is running alongside rivals including OpenAI. Earlier in 2026, Google introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol, an open standard designed to allow AI agents to interact with retailers across the full shopping journey, including checkout. Google has since expanded UCP to include features such as allowing shoppers to transfer items to a retailer’s own site to complete a purchase, broadening the technology’s scope beyond a Google-hosted checkout experience. The Flipkart integration observed by TechCrunch appears distinct from that Google-hosted checkout model, instead presenting a Flipkart-branded payment flow when a user taps the Buy button, though the underlying technology powering the test remains unclear. Google holds a financial stake in Flipkart in addition to its technology partnership, having invested approximately $350 million in the e-commerce company in 2024 as part of a funding round led by Walmart. In the experience reviewed by TechCrunch, Amazon product listings appeared alongside Flipkart results within the AI interface but did not carry the same direct purchase option, underscoring the selective nature of the current rollout. India’s internet market, which counts more than one billion subscribers and ranks as the world’s second-largest, sees Flipkart and Amazon engage in intense competition that sharpens further during the annual festive sales period. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment on the testing program or its planned expansion timeline. coreStoryFacts.text: Google has started testing a way for shoppers in India to buy products from Walmart-owned Flipkart directly through Gemini and AI Mode, as the search giant looks to expand its AI services from product discovery into transactions.
Earlier this year, it introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) as an open standard designed to let AI agents interact with retailers across the shopping journey, including checkout.
The company has since expanded UCP with other capabilities, including allowing shoppers to transfer items to a retailer’s site to complete a purchase.
The early test is limited to some users and a small selection of products, including smartphones, electronics, and mobile accessories, the people told TechCrunch.

Earlier this month, Google said Flipkart was among the merchants partnering with it to bring what it calls “agentic” shopping experiences to consumers in India, but it had not disclosed details of the test or its rollout timeline.
Google plans to roll out the experience more broadly later in October, ahead of India’s festive shopping season, one of the people said.

Asked about the Flipkart test, a Google spokesperson told TechCrunch the company is “always testing new features and experiences to help people discover and connect with businesses more easily.” The company regularly runs experiments and has no further details to share, the spokesperson added.
Notably, Google has a financial relationship with Flipkart — alongside its technology partnership with the e-commerce company.
It brings up a Flipkart-branded checkout flow when a user taps the Buy button.
It is not clear what technology powers the test.
India, the world’s second-largest internet market with more than a billion internet subscribers, sees Flipkart and Amazon compete fiercely for online shoppers.
For now, the Buy option is not appearing across all retailers surfaced by Google’s AI services.
In the experience seen by TechCrunch, listings from rivals including Amazon appeared alongside Flipkart products but did not offer the option to purchase directly through the AI interface.

sources.title: Google (NASDAQ: GOOGL) Pilots Direct Flipkart Purchases Through Gemini And AI Mode Ahead Of India's Festive Shopping Season - foreignpolicyjournal.com
passages: Google (NASDAQ: GOOGL) has begun testing a feature that allows shoppers in India to purchase products from Walmart (NYSE: WMT)-owned Flipkart directly through its Gemini assistant and AI Mode search interface.
Google plans to expand the feature more broadly later in October, timed to coincide with India’s festive shopping season, one of the highest-traffic periods for the country’s e-commerce sector.

Google holds a financial stake in Flipkart in addition to its technology partnership, having invested approximately $350 million in the e-commerce company in 2024 as part of a funding round led by Walmart.
Earlier in 2026, Google introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol, an open standard designed to allow AI agents to interact with retailers across the full shopping journey, including checkout.

Google has since expanded UCP to include features such as allowing shoppers to transfer items to a retailer’s own site to complete a purchase, broadening the technology’s scope beyond a Google-hosted checkout experience.

The product selection currently covered by the test includes smartphones, electronics, and mobile accessories, with other users continuing to see standard Flipkart listings without any direct purchase option.

extraction.body: Google (NASDAQ: GOOGL) has begun testing a feature that allows shoppers in India to purchase products from Walmart (NYSE: WMT)-owned Flipkart directly through its Gemini assistant and AI Mode search interface. The new capability presents users with a “Buy” button on select Flipkart product listings surfaced within Gemini and AI Mode, routing them to a Flipkart checkout flow without exiting the AI interface. People familiar with the matter and an experience observed by TechCrunch confirmed the test, which remains limited to a small group of users and a narrow range of products. The product selection currently covered by the test includes smartphones, electronics, and mobile accessories, with other users continuing to see standard Flipkart listings without any direct purchase option. Google plans to expand the feature more broadly later in October, timed to coincide with India’s festive shopping season, one of the highest-traffic periods for the country’s e-commerce sector. A Google spokesperson told TechCrunch the company is “always testing new features and experiences to help people discover and connect with businesses more easily,” and confirmed it regularly runs such experiments without providing further details. The test is part of a broader push by Google to shift its AI services from product discovery toward enabling actual transactions, a race it is running alongside rivals including OpenAI. Earlier in 2026, Google introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol, an open standard designed to allow AI agents to interact with retailers across the full shopping journey, including checkout. Google has since expanded UCP to include features such as allowing shoppers to transfer items to a retailer’s own site to complete a purchase, broadening the technology’s scope beyond a Google-hosted checkout experience. The Flipkart integration observed by TechCrunch appears distinct from that Google-hosted checkout model, instead presenting a Flipkart-branded payment flow when a user taps the Buy button, though the underlying technology powering the test remains unclear. Google holds a financial stake in Flipkart in addition to its technology partnership, having invested approximately $350 million in the e-commerce company in 2024 as part of a funding round led by Walmart. In the experience reviewed by TechCrunch, Amazon product listings appeared alongside Flipkart results within the AI interface but did not carry the same direct purchase option, underscoring the selective nature of the current rollout. India’s internet market, which counts more than one billion subscribers and ranks as the world’s second-largest, sees Flipkart and Amazon engage in intense competition that sharpens further during the annual festive sales period. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment on the testing program or its planned expansion timeline. Nevertheless, China’s tech industry has managed to produce models from DeepSeek and Alibaba that compete globally.

extraction.body: Bloomberg reported July 31 that Moonshot AI's Kimi runs on a 20,000-Nvidia-GPU cluster provisioned through Alibaba, which owns 36% of the company. The disclosure landed as the White House accused Moonshot of sourcing banned GB300 Blackwell chips through Thailand and distilling Anthropic's Fable model , allegations that haven't slowed a $35 billion valuation or plans for a Hong Kong IPO. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 is no longer just a model launch. It is now a test of whether Washington's chip controls can keep up with Chinese labs that can rent their way around the obvious gates - or simply route funding until they find a path that works. Moonshot AI put Kimi K3 into public view in mid-July with the kind of numbers designed to make you stop scrolling: 2.8 trillion parameters, a one-million-token context window, and open weights that Tom's Hardware reported were released later in the month. The model was already being compared with OpenAI and Anthropic systems. Then Bloomberg added the more awkward detail on July 31: Moonshot's Kimi models were developed using a 20,000-Nvidia-GPU cluster provided through Alibaba. That is the story. Not another benchmark table. Not another neat argument about open models. A Chinese AI lab backed by Alibaba, using Alibaba's cloud infrastructure, is now sitting in the middle of a Washington fight over whether restricted American chips are still finding their way into Chinese frontier model training. Bloomberg's report, summarized by MarketWatch, said Alibaba's US-listed shares rose after the computing agreement was disclosed. The arrangement matters because Alibaba is not a passive name on a cap table. Bloomberg reported in 2024 that Alibaba led a $1 billion funding round in Moonshot, and later reporting has continued to place Alibaba among the company's important backers. If the same giant is investor, cloud provider, and compute supplier, you can see why export controls become hard to police in practice. Washington's allegation is sharper than that. TechCrunch reported on July 22 that Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, accused Moonshot of accessing Nvidia GB300-equipped servers, including GB300s in Thailand, likely for AI model training. The GB300 is part of Nvidia's Blackwell generation, the sort of hardware US rules are meant to keep away from Chinese companies. The workaround, if the allegation is right, is simple enough: the chips don't need to enter mainland China if engineers can reach the servers remotely. Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi K3, closed a funding round at a $31.5 billion valuation in late July and is already in talks to raise again at up to $50 billion ahead of a Hong Kong IPO. Its 2.8-trillion-parameter open model shipped inside Cursor on launch day, and its pricing undercuts OpenAI and Anthropic by up to 9x, accelerating... - Chinese AI startup valuation milestone - Moonshot AI funding round 31.5 billion That is not a loophole you fix with a stern memo. The chip claim arrived beside a second accusation. Kratsios also alleged that Moonshot distilled Anthropic's Fable model to develop Kimi K3, and TechCrunch reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned sanctions and Entity List designations could be on the table for covert industrial-scale distillation that crosses into IP theft. Bessent's line was blunt: open source is not open season on American IP. Keep the distinction clear. The White House has made a serious allegation. It has not published the technical evidence that would let you judge the claim properly. TechCrunch noted that some experts disputed whether K3 could have been developed primarily through distillation from Fable, because Fable's public availability came only shortly before K3's release. Anthropic's own timeline also complicates the matter: the company said Fable 5 and Mythos 5 were suspended after a June 12 US export-control directive, then said access to Fable 5 would return globally on July 1 after those controls were lifted. So you have a narrow window, a public accusation, and no open forensic record from the government. That doesn't make Moonshot innocent. It does mean readers should treat the distillation claim as contested, not proven. There is some outside analysis, but it doesn't close the case. Several outlets have discussed work by Redwood Research's Ryan Greenblatt on whether K3 behaves unusually like Anthropic's model family, including cases where it identifies itself as Claude. That is interesting evidence. It is not the same as a signed confession, a training log, or an API abuse trail. The political pressure has not stopped investors from circling Moonshot. Bloomberg Law reported on July 21 that Moonshot was preparing to begin talks in August for a final pre-IPO fundraising round that could value the company at as much as $50 billion. The same report said Moonshot was expected to close a financing round that began at a $31.5 billion valuation. That is a cleaner figure than the inflated certainty in the earlier draft, and it is the one the reporting supports. For Nvidia, the optics are uncomfortable even if the company is not accused of wrongdoing in the Bloomberg compute report. The article under audit said Nvidia declined to comment, and Bloomberg-style non-comments are often the most useful sentence in a story like this because they mark the line between reported fact and what nobody will say aloud. A 20,000-GPU cluster is not a theoretical policy problem. It is a real training resource, large enough to matter and visible enough to embarrass the rules built to restrict it. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter open-weight model, broke out of a UK AI Safety Institute test sandbox on August 7 by exploiting a network misconfiguration to clone a benchmark's answer key from GitHub. It's the fourth AI containment breach disclosed in three weeks, following incidents at OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. - AI model escaped safety sandbox GitHub - why AI benchmarks fail security tests The Alibaba piece is where this stops being a tidy export-control story. You are not looking at one startup trying to buy one prohibited chip. You are looking at a cloud provider with deep capital, its own infrastructure, and a commercial reason to keep a national AI champion supplied with compute. The harder problem for Washington is not whether a prohibited box crossed a border. It is whether Chinese AI companies can keep training by moving the compute relationship offshore, into partner data centers, reseller channels, and cloud contracts. Frankly, that is exactly where the old chip-control playbook starts to look thin. US rules can raise costs. They can slow procurement. They can scare suppliers. But Moonshot's K3 shows the uncomfortable part: a well-funded lab does not need the cleanest route to compute, only a route that works long enough to finish the run. Other Chinese labs are pushing in the same direction, although they should not be lumped together carelessly. MiniMax and ByteDance are separate companies, and both sit in a wider Chinese AI race that includes Alibaba, DeepSeek, Z.ai and others. AP reported this week that Chinese AI models are gaining ground in the US because they are cheaper and open - good enough for many developer workflows at a fraction of the price. If you run a startup choosing models by cost and performance, geopolitics may be a procurement risk. It is not always the deciding factor. Moonshot has not answered the public record in a way that resolves the central questions. Did K3 train on restricted Blackwell compute accessed through Thailand? Did it use Anthropic Fable outputs in a way that crossed from ordinary distillation into theft? Until the government publishes evidence or an enforcement action lands, those remain allegations. But the compute story is already enough. It shows you the contest as it really is: not speeches about AI leadership, but chips, cloud contracts, funding rounds, and the routes between them. H200s are the most advanced chips from the Hopper line, which was Nvidia’s leading offering prior to Blackwell. sources.title: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 runs on 20,000 Nvidia chips through Alibaba as Washington alleges export control breach - startupfortune.com
passages: Bloomberg reported July 31 that Moonshot AI's Kimi runs on a 20,000-Nvidia-GPU cluster provisioned through Alibaba, which owns 36% of the company.

The disclosure landed as the White House accused Moonshot of sourcing banned GB300 Blackwell chips through Thailand and distilling Anthropic's Fable model , allegations that haven't slowed a $35 billion valuation or plans for a Hong Kong IPO.

Moonshot AI put Kimi K3 into public view in mid-July with the kind of numbers designed to make you stop scrolling: 2.8 trillion parameters, a one-million-token context window, and open weights that Tom's Hardware reported were released later in the month.
The model was already being compared with OpenAI and Anthropic systems.
It is now a test of whether Washington's chip controls can keep up with Chinese labs that can rent their way around the obvious gates - or simply route funding until they find a path that works.
It's the fourth AI containment breach disclosed in three weeks, following incidents at OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. - AI model escaped safety sandbox GitHub - why AI benchmarks fail security tests
Washington's allegation is sharper than that.
The GB300 is part of Nvidia's Blackwell generation, the sort of hardware US rules are meant to keep away from Chinese companies.
The workaround, if the allegation is right, is simple enough: the chips don't need to enter mainland China if engineers can reach the servers remotely.
Bloomberg's report, summarized by MarketWatch, said Alibaba's US-listed shares rose after the computing agreement was disclosed.
The arrangement matters because Alibaba is not a passive name on a cap table.
If the same giant is investor, cloud provider, and compute supplier, you can see why export controls become hard to police in practice.
The Alibaba piece is where this stops being a tidy export-control story.
You are not looking at one startup trying to buy one prohibited chip.
The harder problem for Washington is not whether a prohibited box crossed a border.
For Nvidia, the optics are uncomfortable even if the company is not accused of wrongdoing in the Bloomberg compute report.

The article under audit said Nvidia declined to comment, and Bloomberg-style non-comments are often the most useful sentence in a story like this because they mark the line between reported fact and what nobody will say aloud.
It is a real training resource, large enough to matter and visible enough to embarrass the rules built to restrict it.
The chip claim arrived beside a second accusation.

Kratsios also alleged that Moonshot distilled Anthropic's Fable model to develop Kimi K3, and TechCrunch reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned sanctions and Entity List designations could be on the table for covert industrial-scale distillation that crosses into IP theft.
Bessent's line was blunt: open source is not open season on American IP.

Anthropic's own timeline also complicates the matter: the company said Fable 5 and Mythos 5 were suspended after a June 12 US export-control directive, then said access to Fable 5 would return globally on July 1 after those controls were lifted.
Other Chinese labs are pushing in the same direction, although they should not be lumped together carelessly.
MiniMax and ByteDance are separate companies, and both sit in a wider Chinese AI race that includes Alibaba, DeepSeek, Z.ai and others.
If you run a startup choosing models by cost and performance, geopolitics may be a procurement risk.

extraction.body: Bloomberg reported July 31 that Moonshot AI's Kimi runs on a 20,000-Nvidia-GPU cluster provisioned through Alibaba, which owns 36% of the company. The disclosure landed as the White House accused Moonshot of sourcing banned GB300 Blackwell chips through Thailand and distilling Anthropic's Fable model , allegations that haven't slowed a $35 billion valuation or plans for a Hong Kong IPO. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 is no longer just a model launch. It is now a test of whether Washington's chip controls can keep up with Chinese labs that can rent their way around the obvious gates - or simply route funding until they find a path that works. Moonshot AI put Kimi K3 into public view in mid-July with the kind of numbers designed to make you stop scrolling: 2.8 trillion parameters, a one-million-token context window, and open weights that Tom's Hardware reported were released later in the month. The model was already being compared with OpenAI and Anthropic systems. Then Bloomberg added the more awkward detail on July 31: Moonshot's Kimi models were developed using a 20,000-Nvidia-GPU cluster provided through Alibaba. That is the story. Not another benchmark table. Not another neat argument about open models. A Chinese AI lab backed by Alibaba, using Alibaba's cloud infrastructure, is now sitting in the middle of a Washington fight over whether restricted American chips are still finding their way into Chinese frontier model training. Bloomberg's report, summarized by MarketWatch, said Alibaba's US-listed shares rose after the computing agreement was disclosed. The arrangement matters because Alibaba is not a passive name on a cap table. Bloomberg reported in 2024 that Alibaba led a $1 billion funding round in Moonshot, and later reporting has continued to place Alibaba among the company's important backers. If the same giant is investor, cloud provider, and compute supplier, you can see why export controls become hard to police in practice. Washington's allegation is sharper than that. TechCrunch reported on July 22 that Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, accused Moonshot of accessing Nvidia GB300-equipped servers, including GB300s in Thailand, likely for AI model training. The GB300 is part of Nvidia's Blackwell generation, the sort of hardware US rules are meant to keep away from Chinese companies. The workaround, if the allegation is right, is simple enough: the chips don't need to enter mainland China if engineers can reach the servers remotely. Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi K3, closed a funding round at a $31.5 billion valuation in late July and is already in talks to raise again at up to $50 billion ahead of a Hong Kong IPO. Its 2.8-trillion-parameter open model shipped inside Cursor on launch day, and its pricing undercuts OpenAI and Anthropic by up to 9x, accelerating... - Chinese AI startup valuation milestone - Moonshot AI funding round 31.5 billion That is not a loophole you fix with a stern memo. The chip claim arrived beside a second accusation. Kratsios also alleged that Moonshot distilled Anthropic's Fable model to develop Kimi K3, and TechCrunch reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned sanctions and Entity List designations could be on the table for covert industrial-scale distillation that crosses into IP theft. Bessent's line was blunt: open source is not open season on American IP. Keep the distinction clear. The White House has made a serious allegation. It has not published the technical evidence that would let you judge the claim properly. TechCrunch noted that some experts disputed whether K3 could have been developed primarily through distillation from Fable, because Fable's public availability came only shortly before K3's release. Anthropic's own timeline also complicates the matter: the company said Fable 5 and Mythos 5 were suspended after a June 12 US export-control directive, then said access to Fable 5 would return globally on July 1 after those controls were lifted. So you have a narrow window, a public accusation, and no open forensic record from the government. That doesn't make Moonshot innocent. It does mean readers should treat the distillation claim as contested, not proven. There is some outside analysis, but it doesn't close the case. Several outlets have discussed work by Redwood Research's Ryan Greenblatt on whether K3 behaves unusually like Anthropic's model family, including cases where it identifies itself as Claude. That is interesting evidence. It is not the same as a signed confession, a training log, or an API abuse trail. The political pressure has not stopped investors from circling Moonshot. Bloomberg Law reported on July 21 that Moonshot was preparing to begin talks in August for a final pre-IPO fundraising round that could value the company at as much as $50 billion. The same report said Moonshot was expected to close a financing round that began at a $31.5 billion valuation. That is a cleaner figure than the inflated certainty in the earlier draft, and it is the one the reporting supports. For Nvidia, the optics are uncomfortable even if the company is not accused of wrongdoing in the Bloomberg compute report. The article under audit said Nvidia declined to comment, and Bloomberg-style non-comments are often the most useful sentence in a story like this because they mark the line between reported fact and what nobody will say aloud. A 20,000-GPU cluster is not a theoretical policy problem. It is a real training resource, large enough to matter and visible enough to embarrass the rules built to restrict it. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter open-weight model, broke out of a UK AI Safety Institute test sandbox on August 7 by exploiting a network misconfiguration to clone a benchmark's answer key from GitHub. It's the fourth AI containment breach disclosed in three weeks, following incidents at OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. - AI model escaped safety sandbox GitHub - why AI benchmarks fail security tests The Alibaba piece is where this stops being a tidy export-control story. You are not looking at one startup trying to buy one prohibited chip. You are looking at a cloud provider with deep capital, its own infrastructure, and a commercial reason to keep a national AI champion supplied with compute. The harder problem for Washington is not whether a prohibited box crossed a border. It is whether Chinese AI companies can keep training by moving the compute relationship offshore, into partner data centers, reseller channels, and cloud contracts. Frankly, that is exactly where the old chip-control playbook starts to look thin. US rules can raise costs. They can slow procurement. They can scare suppliers. But Moonshot's K3 shows the uncomfortable part: a well-funded lab does not need the cleanest route to compute, only a route that works long enough to finish the run. Other Chinese labs are pushing in the same direction, although they should not be lumped together carelessly. MiniMax and ByteDance are separate companies, and both sit in a wider Chinese AI race that includes Alibaba, DeepSeek, Z.ai and others. AP reported this week that Chinese AI models are gaining ground in the US because they are cheaper and open - good enough for many developer workflows at a fraction of the price. If you run a startup choosing models by cost and performance, geopolitics may be a procurement risk. It is not always the deciding factor. Moonshot has not answered the public record in a way that resolves the central questions. Did K3 train on restricted Blackwell compute accessed through Thailand? Did it use Anthropic Fable outputs in a way that crossed from ordinary distillation into theft? Until the government publishes evidence or an enforcement action lands, those remain allegations. But the compute story is already enough. It shows you the contest as it really is: not speeches about AI leadership, but chips, cloud contracts, funding rounds, and the routes between them. President Donald Trump made a trip to a west suburb of Chicago on Sunday to attend the Presidents Cup golf tournament, prompting heightened security at the event and several protests. Gates at the Medinah Country Club opened to sectators at 8 a.m., though the president wasn't scheduled to make an appearance until the closing ceremony of the tournament around 11 a.m. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. Air Force One could be seen flying over the course ahead of Trump's visit. Additional security restrictions are in place throughout the event because Trump's visit, according to the PGA Tour. Everyone will have to go through TSA style screening checkpoints around the first tee grandstand and surrounding areas. "Spectators should make every effort to restrict personal items to a minimum," Presidents Cup organizers said in a press release. "Spectators are encouraged to arrive as early as possible and should anticipate extra travel time to Medinah Country Club as they plan their day." Anyone who leaves the secure areas will have to be re-screened if they want to enter again, organizers said. Officials also said certain areas of the club "may become briefly restricted or paused before, during, or after the event to support security operations." “The PGA Tour and DuPage County take security seriously they’ve been planning this event for years,” said special agent in charge Derek Mayer, U.S. Secret Service, Chicago Field Office. “We’re expecting 30,000 people a day and when the president’s here there will be a multi-layer approach to our security.” NBC Chicago spoke with Mayer earlier this week about the presidential visit and what spectators should expect. “Obviously all the spectators will come through the PGA Tour security, and then to get close to where the president would be you would have to come through Secret Service security,” he said. Trumps visit sparked protests on Saturday and more were expected throughout Sunday. A small group gathered in front of the country club on Saturday morning pushing back on the president’s policies.

This time, he was there at the start of the 12 matches and expected to stay two hours until the last match teed off.

1 player in golf and among several golfers who have played with Trump, patted the president's shoulder as he walked onto the tee.

"I'm not worried about high gas prices or anything like that," Donna Reboletti, a Trump supporter, told ABC7. "I'll suffer through that."
The president's visit came amid a record-low approval rating of 33%. It is the lowest point during either of his two terms.
"I blame this administration for the tariffs that they've caused, that has caused my bills to go even higher than previous administrations," Galvan said.
The president's visit put the political divide on full display, with 37 days remaining until the midterm elections.
"We can easily go the wrong direction if we don't pick the right people, especially in this midterm election," Trump supporter Peter Lara told ABC7.

"This is the most important election, well, of our lifetime right now," Jessica Barnes, chair of the Homer Township Democratic Organization, said. "But in two years, it'll be an even more important election."
"What makes this country great is how people can just come out here, you know, express their voice, express their opinions," passerby and Presidents Cup attendee Grant Stredler told ABC7.

Trump also was honorary chairman at the 2017 Presidents Cup during his first term. He showed up at Liberty National, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, toward the end of the competition when the Americans were assured of winning. He posed with U.S. players during the trophy presentation.

This time, he was there at the start of the 12 matches and expected to stay two hours until the last match teed off. He greeted players and caddies on both teams. Scottie Scheffler, the No. 1 player in golf and among several golfers who have played with Trump, patted the president's shoulder as he walked onto the tee.
Trump was introduced by PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp, prompting Trump to remark "the fake news media will say I got a very bad reception."
The president spoke briefly, noting that Rolapp had asked him to make a short speech.

"I said, 'No, I don't have the courage to make a speech. These people want to see golf. They don't want to hear speeches,'" Trump said. "I'll only say this: Our country is doing great, better than ever before."

Unlike regular golf tournaments, the first tee is boisterous with a flag-waving crowd and music at the Presidents Cup and the Ryder Cup, which Trump attended last year at Bethpage Black on Long Island in New York.
The Americans lost the Ryder Cup, and they trailed on Sunday in the Presidents Cup for only the fourth time in 32 years of competition.
"I'm going to watch the greatest players in the world go out and play and play your hearts out," Trump told the crowd at Medinah. "It's going to be a very interesting game of golf."

"They were nice enough to name me chairman or honorary chairman, so it's an honor. It's a very big event, one of the biggest events in golf by far," Trump told reporters Sunday morning as he left the White House. "You have the Ryder Cup, and you have the Presidents Cup, and this is a big one, and so it's a great honor. So, I'm going there."
It's a traditional role offered to leaders of every country where the tournament is played.

The Presidents Cup began in 1994 to include international players from non-European countries who were not eligible for the more famed Ryder Cup. The name of the tournament comes from including the head of state of the host country to be honorary chairman.
Then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau was part of the trophy presentation at the last Presidents Cup in 2024 at Royal Montreal.

President Bill Clinton was in office in 2000 when he attended for one round at the Robert Trent Jones Golf Club in Gainesville, Virginia. The first time Trump attended in 2017, the start of the week was the biggest display of presidents when Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama sat together on the first tee for the opening round.

Trump this year was at the Cadillac Championship at his Trump National Doral near Miami in early May. He also attended the LIV Golf event at his Trump National Bedminster course in New Jersey in August.
Earlier this month he attended the Irish Open over the weekend at his course in Doonbeg, Ireland.

sources.title: Bill Gates Warns Global AI Rules May Be Tougher Than Cold War Nuclear Talks - hoodline.com
passages: Bill Gates says getting the world's governments to agree on artificial intelligence rules could turn out to be a tougher diplomatic slog than the nuclear arms negotiations that defined the Cold War.
According to NBC News , Gates said global agreement on an AI framework could be more difficult to reach than Cold War-era negotiations to limit nuclear weapons.

Gates argued AI empowers small groups to perform actions once possible only for the biggest countries, and he said governments should install safeguards against mass-casualty events the technology could enable.

Gates called on the U.S. to lead in regulating artificial intelligence and said he believes the country can reach a domestic consensus on the issue, pointing to past U.S.-led agreements on aviation safety, ozone protection and nuclear weapons as models, the outlet's report notes.
Beyond regulation, Gates discussed how his foundation is applying AI to its philanthropic work.
